title: Epochal context stress & streaming shear — Product walkthrough
summary: Redwood AE+SE ran a focused demo showing how Redwood handles multi-hour conversational history, high TPS bursts, and streaming backpressure. Customer is evaluating for a production migration for chat-based retail assistants that keep long user histories. Discussion covered Dedicated vs Hosted, VPC, KV cache behavior, quantization tradeoffs, and telemetry for alerts. Agreed to run a 2-week pilot and a short benchmark using Lumina sample prompts.
topics: High TPS surge handling and graceful degradation
Console walkthrough: Optimize recommendations and rollouts
action_items: Jordan Lee: Share tailored latency/cost spreadsheet and pilot onboarding doc (due: 2027-10-14)
Priya Nair: Provide step-by-step runbook for KV cache prefix tuning and eviction flags (due: 2027-10-15)
Evan Park / Lumina: Provide 2 canonical prompt templates and 5k sample chat histories for benchmark (due: 2027-10-18)
Amira Hassan: Confirm compliance requirements (data residency/SOC2 scope) and share checklist (due: 2027-10-16)
next_steps: Redwood to provision pilot environment (dedicated vCPU/GPU slice) and run 48h soak
Lumina to share sample traffic pattern and SSO details for access
Schedule technical deep dive focused on telemetry and alerts (Priya to lead)
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-10-11 11:00 PT
Duration: 58 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Jordan Lee, Priya Nair (Redwood); Carlos Mendez, Amira Hassan, Evan Park (Lumina)
Links: demo deck (shared), pilot onboarding doc (to be shared)

[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — Jordan from Redwood, I'm the AE, with Priya our solutions eng. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Carlos Mendez: Good, thanks. Excited to see the long-history stuff. We have a bunch of edge cases where sessions can be hours long and then get a huge surge.
[00:12] Priya Nair: Cool, we'll dive in. High level agenda: show API behavior with very long context, then a simulated TPS surge with streaming backpressure, and then the Console / Optimize suggestions for cost/latency.
[00:22] Evan Park: Quick note, our typical session history is about 30 to 90 minutes, but power users can have 4+ hour sessions with multiple turns.
[00:27] Amira Hassan: Also, security is a blocker — we need to see VPC and KMS options, audit logs, SSO.
[00:32] Jordan Lee: Totally. We'll cover Private options and the audit paths near the end. Ok Priya, want to kick off the demo?

[01:00] Priya Nair: Yep. I'm going to share my screen — starting with a synthetic workload runner hitting Redwood API directly. Note: the model variant here is the 'long-history optimized' profile.
[01:12] (screen share starts)
[01:15] Priya Nair: First test is a 200k token rolling history across 12k concurrent sessions, but per-session TPS low — we want to see KV cache warm and eviction patterns. You might see some tokenization artifacts in the transcript — that's expected for synthetic prompts.
[01:30] Carlos Mendez: Wait 200k tokens? Are you summing per-user history or global? That seems huge.
[01:36] Priya Nair: That's total retained history for the cluster, we emulate long prefix windows per user. Redwood uses prefix/KV caching to avoid re-executing early layers — the K-V cash, sometimes auto-transcribes it as K-V cash — it's pronounced K-V cache.
[01:48] Evan Park: We've seen other vendors drop context aggressively, we need the system to degrade gracefully.

[02:12] Priya Nair: Right. For graceful degradation we demonstrated two levers: automatic prefix truncation with score-based summary, and a circuit-breaker that switch routes to a cheaper quantized variant under backpressure.
[02:27] Amira Hassan: Can you show that fallback? That's crucial for us.
[02:30] Priya Nair: Absolutely. I'm going to start a 10k TPS burst from the runner and introduce artificial network jitter to force streaming backpressure.
[02:45] (noise; typing)
[03:02] Priya Nair: Starting burst now — you'll see streaming responses slow and then a seamless fallback to a lower-cost shard.
[03:10] (simulated traffic shown)
[03:17] Jordan Lee: You'll see in Console we have a rule — policy named "surge-fallback-v1" — it routes by latency SLO and cost threshold. Under the hood it can switch to a quantized int8/nf4-style variant; sometimes we call it n-four, the naming in the UI is shorthand.
[03:33] Carlos Mendez: How do you ensure quality doesn't tank when you switch? We can't afford hallucinations in product descriptions.
[03:39] Priya Nair: Two pieces. One, model selection based on similarity of logits and baseline evals tied to your prompt set; two, automatic A/B canary where a small percentage still hits the higher quality model and we do online evals. The optimize dashboard surfaces regression alerts if score drops.
[03:58] Evan Park: Are those evals configurable with our own test prompts?
[04:02] Priya Nair: Yes — you can upload prompt families; Optimize runs periodic checks and triggers alerts and optional rollback.

[04:30] Amira Hassan: Timings — what's the expected added latency when we use the fallback?
[04:35] Priya Nair: Typically the quantized route is slightly faster but may have a small delta on tricky completion quality. Under backpressure the overall end-to-end latency improves because requests are queued less. In experiments we saw 25-40% fewer tail spikes.

[05:12] Jordan Lee: Wanted to call out autoscaling — for Dedicated we can provision burst capacity and set a floor. For Hosted we have region-based fallbacks. Which deployment are you leaning to?
[05:22] Carlos Mendez: We're evaluating Dedicated because of PII and compliance, but we'll consider Hosted for initial rollout if the economics look right.
[05:29] Amira Hassan: Dedicated + VPC is the preferred path, yes. Do you have SSO and SAML examples in the docs?
[05:34] Jordan Lee: Yes, we have an SSO guide and audit logs accessible via the console or exported to your SIEM. I'll attach those.

[06:05] Priya Nair: Back to the demo — now I'm toggling KV cache eviction to 'aggressive' to show behavior when memory is constrained. You'll see older prefixes evicted and a small quality delta on early-turn recall.
[06:22] (beep)
[06:30] Evan Park: When the KV cache evicts, do you recompute the full history or is there a summary fallback?
[06:35] Priya Nair: We do both options — either roll-up summaries (we call it compaction) or a hard truncate. The roll-up is best for recall with less token overhead.

[07:00] (screen; console graphs)
[07:12] Priya Nair: Here's the Console trace: token-level latency, per-route costs, prefix hit ratio. There's also a timeline where you can replay the traffic and see which sessions were rerouted.
[07:24] Carlos Mendez: That replay is useful. Can you export traces to our datadog?
[07:28] Priya Nair: Yup, export hooks to Datadog and Splunk and you can ship raw request traces to your S3 as well.

[08:10] Jordan Lee: Quick digression on billing — we bill token-in and token-out, but during fallback the token cost changes by model variant. We'll show the spreadsheet after.
[08:22] Amira Hassan: On encryption — keys in KMS? HSM?
[08:25] Jordan Lee: Both; you can bring-your-own-KMS and we integrate with common cloud KMS providers. HSM is available for Private deployments.

[09:02] Priya Nair: Now I'm going to simulate intermittent stream timeouts — introducing a 5s stall on the stream and a client-side connection with 15s keepalive.
[09:12] (pause)
[09:18] Priya Nair: With our streaming API, we surface partial deltas and you can resume using session IDs; we also have TTLs on in-memory session windows. If a stream stalls past a configured threshold we move to chunked second-phase completion — that's the graceful degrade mode.
[09:35] Evan Park: Do you persist tokens to disk during resume?
[09:39] Priya Nair: We persist indices to a fast KV store; full tensors remain in GPU memory while active. On resume we cold-load from the persisted KV, which adds some latency but keeps correctness.

[10:00] Carlos Mendez: For our app, tail latency matters — we need 95th < 250ms for short queries and sub-second for multi-turn. Can you meet that with long contexts?
[10:11] Priya Nair: We tune batching windows and route short queries to low-latency lanes with prefetched KV; for long-context completions we recommend relaxed SLOs and progressive streaming. The Console Optimize tab will suggest batch sizes and max sequence lengths per model to hit your SLO vs cost target.
[10:30] Jordan Lee: Also note that you can set per-route SLO policies so chat endpoint A gets one routing and FAQ endpoint B gets another.

[11:00] (customer side discussion)
[11:12] Amira Hassan: One thing I'm worried about is telemetry noise. If the system tries to fallback too often it will create false positives.
[11:20] Priya Nair: Good point — Optimize includes hysteresis and sliding-window thresholds for alerts; you can tune sensitivity and add business-rule filters.

[12:00] (demo continues; we jump ahead a bit)
[12:32] Priya Nair: I'm now showing a benchmark chart: baseline vs fallback scenarios. Under a 12k TPS spike, system keeps 99.2% success rate with fallback enabled, vs 86% failure rate when naively throttled.
[12:46] Carlos Mendez: That's promising. How reproducible is that with our prompts?
[12:50] Priya Nair: We'll run the benchmark with your sample prompts; that's part of the pilot.

[14:00] Jordan Lee: Quick question for the engineering team — Evan, what are the top three constraints you expect for the pilot?
[14:08] Evan Park: 1) We need representative user histories, 2) realistic concurrency patterns including spikes, and 3) we need the logs to integrate into our observability stack.
[14:16] Jordan Lee: Good — we'll mirror those.

[15:00] Priya Nair: Switching to Console Optimize now — it gives us recommended quant levels, batch sizes, and a simulated cost delta if you change routes. You can preview the effect on token-level cost and expected latency distributions.
[15:20] Amira Hassan: Can the Optimize suggestions be auto-applied? We prefer manual approval but can set safe guards.
[15:25] Priya Nair: They can be auto-applied in a controlled rollout. We also log every change and can set a canary percent for auto-rollouts.

[16:00] (brief crosstalk)
[16:12] Carlos Mendez: Regarding on-prem, do you support air-gapped deployments? We have a partner that requires that.
[16:17] Jordan Lee: Yes — Private on-prem package exists; it requires a short engagement for install and we support KMS with HSM connectors. We'll prepare the packaging checklist.

[17:00] Evan Park: Latency during KV cold-loads — can you quantify?
[17:04] Priya Nair: Cold-loads vary by model size; typical cold-load penalty is 200-600ms depending on sequence length and disk tier. We mitigate with warmers and prefetch heuristics.

[18:00] Jordan Lee: Quick callout — in the pilot we recommend enabling prefix compaction and a 30-minute TTL for inactive sessions as a starting point, then we'll tune.
[18:10] Amira Hassan: Ok that's reasonable.

[19:00] (customer asks about rate-limiting)
[19:06] Priya Nair: You can configure token-level throttles and per-API keys. During surges the system will first apply rate-limiters, then fallback routing, then queuing. We also support soft-queues in Dedicated to preserve throughput.

[20:00] (mid-call break; quick admin)
[21:00] Jordan Lee: Wanted to show the audit logs — here are examples of request/response hashes, user ids pseudonymized, and an export function.
[21:12] Amira Hassan: We need retention to be configurable.
[21:16] Jordan Lee: Yes, retention can be set per-tenant in Private.

[22:30] Priya Nair: Ok, wrapping up the technical piece with a failure-mode table on the screen: timeout -> chunked response; KV eviction -> compaction summary; capacity -> fallback quantized model + burst pool; SLO breach -> route to low-latency lane or degrade.
[22:56] Carlos Mendez: That table is exactly what we need in our runbook.

[24:00] (questions on pricing)
[24:06] Jordan Lee: We'll send a spreadsheet showing host vs dedicated cost curves including the fallback delta. Important to model the canary percent for cost.

[25:30] Amira Hassan: Small nit: some names in the UI were a bit confusing — the variant labels like "n4-quant" don't map to our internal naming. Can we alias names?
[25:38] Priya Nair: Yes, you can set route aliases and explanatory labels in the Console.

[27:00] (closing section)
[27:12] Jordan Lee: Recap: Redwood will run a 48h pilot with Lumina prompts, provide a tuned KV prefix config, and share security docs. Lumina will provide sample histories, confirm compliance needs, and review costs with finance.
[27:30] Carlos Mendez: Sounds good. Two requests: a concise runbook and the pilot checklist.
[27:36] Jordan Lee: We'll send both.

[28:00] (light chatter; meeting ends)

Note: transcription has some mis-hearings (K-V cash, n-four) — verified sections will be in the follow-up doc.

End of transcript.
